Jeffreys divergence estimation.

When the velocity has the affine (linear-in-state) form vc𝒱​(x,t)=Ac,t​x+rc,tv_{c}^{\mathcal{V}}(x,t)=A_{c,t}x+r_{c,t}, we integrate the mean and covariance ODEs in Eq. (14) and evaluate the corresponding Gaussian distance from the resulting moments; Gaussian Jeffreys divergence uses Eq. (16). For an unconstrained velocity—used to estimate Jeffreys divergence and full Fisher information—we instead generate endpoint samples by solving Eq. (1) and evaluate log⁡qc𝒱​(x)\log q_{c}^{\mathcal{V}}(x) through the continuous change-of-variables identity in Eq. (111). Jeffreys divergence is then estimated with Eq. (8).

D.1.3 Gaussian-process with kernel regression

Our implementation follows the GKR code of Ye and Wessel [2025], available at https://github.com/AgeYY/speed˙grid˙cell˙information.

GKR models the smooth conditional response distribution as

qGKR​(x∣u)=𝒩⁡(x∣μ^​(u),Σ^​(u)),q_{\mathrm{GKR}}(x\mid u)=\mathcal{N}\!\left(x\mid\widehat{\mu}(u),\widehat{\Sigma}(u)\right), (135)

Here uu denotes the conditioning input to each fitted GKR model: u=θu=\theta for the Fisher datasets, u=(c,t)u=(c,t) for the synthetic OU datasets, and uu is grating orientation for Stringer. For the Allen two-photon calcium-imaging and Allen Neuropixels ephys datasets, we fit a separate GKR model for each joint drifting-direction–temporal-frequency condition, with u=tu=t within each model. We use an RBF kernel for nonperiodic inputs and a periodic kernel for grating orientation.

Let ri=xi−μ^​(ui)r_{i}=x_{i}-\widehat{\mu}(u_{i}) be the fitted residuals. GKR estimates the conditional covariance by normalized kernel regression of their outer products,

Σ^​(u)=∑i=1nkλ​(ui,u)​ri​ri⊤∑i=1nkλ​(ui,u)+ϵΣ​I.\widehat{\Sigma}(u)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_{\lambda}(u_{i},u)r_{i}r_{i}^{\top}}{\sum_{i=1}^{n}k_{\lambda}(u_{i},u)}+\epsilon_{\Sigma}I. (136)

For the nonperiodic scalar conditions, inputs are standardized and

kλ​(ui,u)=exp⁡[−(u~i−u~)22​(λ+ϵλ)].k_{\lambda}(u_{i},u)=\exp\!\left[-\frac{(\widetilde{u}_{i}-\widetilde{u})^{2}}{2(\lambda+\epsilon_{\lambda})}\right]. (137)

For an orientation with period PP, the periodic covariance kernel is instead

kλper​(ui,u)=exp⁡[−sin2⁡(π⁡(ui−u)/P)λ+ϵλ].k_{\lambda}^{\mathrm{per}}(u_{i},u)=\exp\!\left[-\frac{\sin^{2}\!\left(\pi(u_{i}-u)/P\right)}{\lambda+\epsilon_{\lambda}}\right]. (138)

The default configuration uses 200200 inducing points; 300300 mean-GP iterations at learning rate 0.050.05; and 3030 covariance-kernel epochs at learning rate 0.10.1, with a validation fraction of 1/31/3.

D.1.4 Wishart-process estimator

Our Wishart process implementation reuses the original JAX/NumPyro model, kernels, variational inference, and posterior-mode prediction from https://github.com/neurostatslab/wishart-process, pinned to commit 5607d14.

The Wishart process models both the mean and covariance of a smoothly condition-dependent Gaussian distribution [Nejatbakhsh et al., 2023]. For a conditioning input uu and response X∈ℝdX\in\mathbb{R}^{d},

X∣u∼𝒩(μ(u),Σ(u)),μj(⋅)∼GP(0,kμ),Fj​p(⋅)∼GP(0,kΣ).{X\mid u\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu(u),\Sigma(u)\right),\qquad\mu_{j}(\cdot)\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,k_{\mu}),\qquad F_{jp}(\cdot)\sim\operatorname{GP}(0,k_{\Sigma}).} (139)

The latent functions μj\mu_{j} model the conditional mean, while the factors Fj​pF_{jp} model the conditional covariance; all mean coordinates and covariance factors have independent GP priors. Let F⁡(u)∈ℝd×dF(u)\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} collect the active covariance factors used by the upstream implementation, which defines

Σ⁡(u)=L⁡[F⁡(u)​F​(u)⊤+δ​Id]​L⊤,δ=0.1.{\Sigma(u)=L\left[F(u)F(u)^{\top}+\delta I_{d}\right]L^{\top},\qquad\delta=0.1.} (140)

The Gram matrix F⁡(u)​F​(u)⊤F(u)F(u)^{\top} is positive semidefinite, and adding δ​Id\delta I_{d} makes it positive definite before scaling by LL. This Gram construction motivates the name Wishart process: at each condition, outer products of Gaussian latent factors form a covariance matrix, while the GP correlations across uu make that covariance vary smoothly with the condition. The shared matrix LL is initialized as the Cholesky factor of (Σ^pool+δ​Id)/(d+1)(\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{pool}}+\delta I_{d})/(d+1), where Σ^pool\widehat{\Sigma}_{\mathrm{pool}} is the pooled within-bin empirical covariance. It is then optimized during SVI.

The mean and covariance-factor GPs use separate product kernels. For r∈{μ,Σ}r\in\{\mu,\Sigma\} and condition coordinate qq,

kr​(u,u′)\displaystyle k_{r}(u,u^{\prime}) =∏qexp[−dq​(uq,uq′)2λr,q]+10−3𝟏{u=u′},\displaystyle=\prod_{q}\exp\!\left[-\frac{d_{q}(u_{q},u_{q}^{\prime})^{2}}{\lambda_{r,q}}\right]+10^{-3}\mathbf{1}\{u=u^{\prime}\}, (141)
dq​(a,b)\displaystyle d_{q}(a,b) ={a−b,for a nonperiodic coordinate,sin⁡(π⁡(a−b)/Pq),for a coordinate with period Pq.\displaystyle=\begin{cases}a-b,&\text{for a nonperiodic coordinate},\\ \sin\!\left(\pi(a-b)/P_{q}\right),&\text{for a coordinate with period $P_{q}$}.\end{cases} (142)

Here λμ,q\lambda_{\mu,q} and λΣ,q\lambda_{\Sigma,q} separately control how smoothly the mean and covariance factors vary along condition coordinate qq: larger widths produce stronger sharing across nearby conditions. The Fisher datsets have one nonperiodic coordinate u=θu=\theta, whereas the Stringer recordings have one periodic orientation coordinate u=θu=\theta with period P=πP=\pi.

The authors’ code interface requires an equal-trial tensor with shape K×C×dK\times C\times d. After fixing the train, validation, and test splits, our wrapper bins only the training observations, sets K=minc⁡ncK=\min_{c}n_{c}, and subsamples every occupied bin to KK responses. All validation and test observations are retained. Mean and covariance kernel widths (λμ,q\lambda_{\mu,q} and λΣ,q\lambda_{\Sigma,q}) are selected by held-out Gaussian log likelihood.

To search kernel widths, we evaluate the grids in Table 3, adaptively expanding the search space when needed. We continue the expansion until the validation curve exhibits an inverted-U shape, indicating a local optimum, or until the kernel width becomes sufficiently large to produce nearly constant smoothing. For example, supplementary Figure S5 shows the resulting search profiles for the Stringer recordings.

For the PCA-70 Allen Neuropixels analysis in Figure 7, we found it practically difficult to identify optimal kernel widths because validation often favored very large values, resulting in estimates that were nearly constant over time. This behavior may reflect the high dimensionality and non-Gaussianity of the neural responses.

Therefore we instead reducing the responses to 10 principal components where the Wishart process produced more reasonable fits, as shown in Supplementary Figure S10. Affine flow matching remains best among Gaussian methods.

D.1.5 Cross-fitted optimal linear estimator (OLE)

We mainly follow Kanitscheider et al. [2015] for the locally optimal linear estimator and its finite-sample bias correction. OLE fits a linear decoder on a training set and projects held-out responses onto the resulting axis. Our reported achieved-information estimate applies the bias correction shown below and is clipped at zero.

Specifically, we estimate this quantity with five-fold cross-fitting independently for each adjacent pair θL<θR\theta_{L}<\theta_{R} on a 31-endpoint grid, where h=θR−θL=0.4h=\theta_{R}-\theta_{L}=0.4. Responses are assigned to disjoint radius-h/2h/2 windows around the two endpoints. If either window contains fewer than eight responses, we instead use the nearest disjoint groups with eight responses per endpoint. For fold ff, four folds estimate the endpoint means and Ledoit–Wolf covariances. We then form

μ^f′\displaystyle\widehat{\mu}_{f}^{\prime} =μ^R,f−μ^L,fh,\displaystyle=\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{R,f}-\widehat{\mu}_{L,f}}{h}, Σ^f\displaystyle\widehat{\Sigma}_{f} =Σ^L,f+Σ^R,f2,\displaystyle=\frac{\widehat{\Sigma}_{L,f}+\widehat{\Sigma}_{R,f}}{2}, (143)
w^f\displaystyle\widehat{w}_{f} =Σ^f−1​μ^f′μ^f′⊤Σ^f−1μ^f′,\displaystyle=\frac{\widehat{\Sigma}_{f}^{-1}\widehat{\mu}_{f}^{\prime}}{\widehat{\mu}_{f}^{\prime}{}^{\top}\widehat{\Sigma}_{f}^{-1}\widehat{\mu}_{f}^{\prime}}, b^f\displaystyle\widehat{b}_{f} =θL+θR2−w^f⊤​μ^L,f+μ^R,f2.\displaystyle=\frac{\theta_{L}+\theta_{R}}{2}-\widehat{w}_{f}^{\top}\frac{\widehat{\mu}_{L,f}+\widehat{\mu}_{R,f}}{2}. (144)

The fitted decoder θ^=w^f⊤​X+b^f\widehat{\theta}=\widehat{w}_{f}^{\top}X+\widehat{b}_{f} is frozen and applied only to the held-out fold. Pooling the five held-out folds therefore evaluates each selected response exactly once out of fold. Let y¯L,y¯R\bar{y}_{L},\bar{y}_{R}, sL2,sR2s_{L}^{2},s_{R}^{2}, and nL,nRn_{L},n_{R} denote the means, sample variances, and counts of the pooled held-out projections. The reported estimate is

I^OLEraw\displaystyle\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{OLE}}^{\mathrm{raw}} =(y¯R−y¯L)2−sL2/nL−sR2/nRh2​(sL2+sR2)/2,\displaystyle=\frac{(\bar{y}_{R}-\bar{y}_{L})^{2}-s_{L}^{2}/n_{L}-s_{R}^{2}/n_{R}}{h^{2}(s_{L}^{2}+s_{R}^{2})/2}, I^OLE\displaystyle\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{OLE}} =max⁡{I^OLEraw,0}.\displaystyle=\max\!\left\{\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{OLE}}^{\mathrm{raw}},0\right\}. (145)

D.1.6 TRE density-ratio estimation for categorical Jeffreys divergence

For the full Jeffreys divergence comparison in Supplementary Figure S1, we use telescoping density-ratio estimation (TRE) [Rhodes et al., 2020] with B∈{1,8,16}B\in\{1,8,16\} bridges. For each unordered pair of categorical conditions aa and bb, TRE draws independent samples Xa∼paX_{a}\sim p_{a} and Xb∼pbX_{b}\sim p_{b} and forms B+1B+1 angular waymarks

Zm=cos(ϕm)Xa+sin(ϕm)Xb,ϕm=m​π2​B,m=0,…,B.{Z_{m}=\cos(\phi_{m})X_{a}+\sin(\phi_{m})X_{b},\qquad\phi_{m}=\frac{m\pi}{2B},\qquad m=0,\ldots,B.} (146)

Then we constructed BB adjacent-ratio classifiers share a three-hidden-layer MLP trunk with width 128128 and use separate linear output heads. Each condition-pair model is trained for at most 10001000 epochs with batch size 512512, AdamW learning rate 10−310^{-3}, zero weight decay, and gradient clipping at norm 1010. We select the checkpoint with the lowest validation loss. If qmq_{m} denotes the density of ZmZ_{m}, classifier head mm is trained with equal class priors to distinguish qmq_{m} from qm+1q_{m+1}. The estimated logits then telescope to

r^a​b​(x)=∑m=0B−1ℓ^a​b,m​(x)≈∑m=0B−1log⁡qm​(x)qm+1​(x)=log⁡pa​(x)pb​(x).{\widehat{r}_{ab}(x)=\sum_{m=0}^{B-1}\widehat{\ell}_{ab,m}(x)\approx\sum_{m=0}^{B-1}\log\frac{q_{m}(x)}{q_{m+1}(x)}=\log\frac{p_{a}(x)}{p_{b}(x)}.} (147)

We estimate the Jeffreys divergence for each condition pair by averaging this log ratio under the two endpoint distributions and clip negative finite-sample estimates at zero:

D^J​(pa,pb)=max⁡{0,1na​∑i=1nar^a​b​(Xa,i)−1nb​∑j=1nbr^a​b​(Xb,j)}.{\widehat{D}_{\mathrm{J}}(p_{a},p_{b})=\max\!\left\{0,\frac{1}{n_{a}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{a}}\widehat{r}_{ab}(X_{a,i})-\frac{1}{n_{b}}\sum_{j=1}^{n_{b}}\widehat{r}_{ab}(X_{b,j})\right\}.} (148)

D.2 Simulation datasets

D.2.1 Categorical RDM dataset

Here, we describe the categorical RDM experiment shown in Figure 3.

We define the conditional response distribution as

z|Y=k∼𝒩⁡(μk,diag⁡(vk)),z\mid Y=k\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu_{k},\operatorname{diag}(v_{k})\right), (149)

where YY is uniformly distributed over {0,…,4}\{0,\ldots,4\} and zz is three-dimensional. We generate the parameters μk\mu_{k} and diag⁡(vk)\operatorname{diag}(v_{k}) once and hold them fixed across all five repetitions. Thus, the repetitions share the same category-conditional distributions and differ only in their sampled observations.

Specifically, we generate μk\mu_{k} and diag⁡(vk)\operatorname{diag}(v_{k}) as follows. We draw each mean coordinate as μk,j=Gk,j​Zk,j\mu_{k,j}=G_{k,j}Z_{k,j}, where Gk,j∼Unif⁡(0.2,2.0)G_{k,j}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0.2,2.0) and Zk,j∼Unif⁡(0,1)Z_{k,j}\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1). We resample the candidate means until every pair is separated by at least 3/2\sqrt{3}/2 (half the diagonal of the unit cube), thereby keeping the components well separated. We set the conditional variances to

vk,j=3​(0.15)2+0.15​|μk,j|+10−5.v_{k,j}=3(0.15)^{2}+0.15|\mu_{k,j}|+10^{-5}. (150)

We then independently draw five datasets from this fixed population. When fitting the structured models—that is, all velocity families in Table 1 except the unconstrained family—we use all observations. Because the response dimension is low, we set λ=0\lambda=0 for affine flow, corresponding to no regularization. The nonlinear Jeffreys model instead uses an 80/20 training–validation split. Figure 3A shows accuracy as a function of sample size, and Figure 3B shows the corresponding RDM estimates at 2,000 total samples.

Figure S1 compares flow matching against plug-in mean estimators for correlation, cosine, and squared Euclidean distance; pooled-covariance Mahalanobis estimators with and without Ledoit–Wolf (LW) shrinkage; a condition-specific LW covariance estimator for Gaussian Jeffreys divergence; and TRE estimators using 1, 8, or 16 bridges for full Jeffreys divergence.

We compute all six ground-truth RDMs analytically from the known population means μk\mu_{k} and diagonal covariances diag⁡(vk)\operatorname{diag}(v_{k}).

We evaluate estimation performance using the mean relative absolute error (MRAE) over the unique off-diagonal category pairs. Let 𝒫={(i,j):0≤i<j≤C−1}\mathcal{P}=\{(i,j):0\leq i<j\leq C-1\} and M=|𝒫|=(C2)M=|\mathcal{P}|=\binom{C}{2}. For an estimated RDM D^\widehat{D} and its ground-truth RDM DD,

MRE⁡(D^,D)=1M​∑(i,j)∈𝒫|D^i​j−Di​j|max⁡{|Di​j|,10−12}.\operatorname{MRE}(\widehat{D},D)=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal{P}}\frac{\left|\widehat{D}_{ij}-D_{ij}\right|}{\max\!\left\{\left|D_{ij}\right|,10^{-12}\right\}}. (151)

With C=5C=5, the average includes M=10M=10 unique category pairs.

D.2.2 Fisher datasets

Here we describe the datasets used for estimating Fisher information in Figure 4A–F. We first specify the Gaussian dataset used for linear Fisher information, then the mixture dataset used for full Fisher information.

Gaussian responses and linear Fisher information.

For the Gaussian dataset (Figure 4A–C), θ∈[−6,6]\theta\in[-6,6], while the response dimension dd follows the sweep protocol below:

pG​(x∣θ)=𝒩⁡(x∣μ⁡(θ),Σ⁡(θ)).p^{\mathrm{G}}(x\mid\theta)=\mathcal{N}\!\left(x\mid\mu(\theta),\Sigma(\theta)\right). (152)

The mean is a Gaussian bump with equal-spacing centers ϑj=−6+12​(j−1)/(d−1)\vartheta_{j}=-6+12(j-1)/(d-1)

μj​(θ)=aj​exp⁡[−0.2​(θ−ϑj)2],\mu_{j}(\theta)=a_{j}\exp\!\left[-0.2\left(\theta-\vartheta_{j}\right)^{2}\right], (153)

where aj​∼iid​Unif⁡(0.2,2.0)a_{j}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}(0.2,2.0). and the condition-dependent diagonal covariance is

[Σ⁡(θ)]j​ℓ=δj​ℓ​[d​(0.07)2+d300​ 1.30​|μj​(θ)|+10−8].\left[\Sigma(\theta)\right]_{j\ell}=\delta_{j\ell}\left[d(0.07)^{2}+\frac{d}{300}\,1.30\lvert\mu_{j}(\theta)\rvert+10^{-8}\right]. (154)

The d/300d/300 factor preserves the relative covariance modulation across response dimensions.

The target is linear Fisher information, μ′​(θ)⊤​Σ​(θ)−1​μ′​(θ)\mu^{\prime}(\theta)^{\top}\Sigma(\theta)^{-1}\mu^{\prime}(\theta), estimated by affine flow (Section D.1.1 and Proposition A.7), GKR (Section D.1.3), the Wishart process (Section D.1.4), and five-fold cross-fitted OLE (Section D.1.5). The sample-size sweep fixes d=300d=300 and uses N∈{500,1000,3000,5000,10000}N\in\{500,1000,3000,5000,10000\}; the dimension sweep fixes N=1000N=1000 and uses d∈{10,20,50,100,200,300,400}d\in\{10,20,50,100,200,300,400\}.

For the affine-flow readout, each adjacent pair (θk,θk+1)(\theta_{k},\theta_{k+1}), with midpoint θ¯k=(θk+θk+1)/2\overline{\theta}_{k}=(\theta_{k}+\theta_{k+1})/2, shares a covariance obtained by averaging its two affine matrices at every flow time:

A¯k,t\displaystyle\overline{A}_{k,t} =12​(Aθk,t+Aθk+1,t),\displaystyle=\tfrac{1}{2}\left(A_{\theta_{k},t}+A_{\theta_{k+1},t}\right), Σ¯˙k,t\displaystyle\dot{\overline{\Sigma}}_{k,t} =A¯k,t​Σ¯k,t+Σ¯k,t​A¯k,t⊤,\displaystyle=\overline{A}_{k,t}\overline{\Sigma}_{k,t}+\overline{\Sigma}_{k,t}\overline{A}_{k,t}^{\top}, Σ¯k,0\displaystyle\overline{\Sigma}_{k,0} =Id,\displaystyle=I_{d}, (155)
I^lin​(θ¯k)\displaystyle\widehat{I}_{\mathrm{lin}}(\overline{\theta}_{k}) =Δ​bk⊤​Σ¯k,1−1​Δ​bk(θk+1−θk)2,\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta b_{k}^{\top}\overline{\Sigma}_{k,1}^{-1}\Delta b_{k}}{(\theta_{k+1}-\theta_{k})^{2}}, Δ​bk\displaystyle\Delta b_{k} =b⁡(θk+1)−b⁡(θk).\displaystyle=b(\theta_{k+1})-b(\theta_{k}). (156)

For estimated Fisher information I^​(θk)\widehat{I}(\theta_{k}) and ground truth I⁡(θk)I(\theta_{k}) at KK evaluation points, we report MRAE

MRAE⁡(I^,I)=1K​∑k=1K|I^​(θk)−I⁡(θk)|max⁡{|I⁡(θk)|,10−12}.\operatorname{MRAE}(\widehat{I},I)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\left|\widehat{I}(\theta_{k})-I(\theta_{k})\right|}{\max\!\left\{\left|I(\theta_{k})\right|,10^{-12}\right\}}. (157)

Mixture responses and full Fisher information.

For the non-Gaussian dataset (Figure 4D–F), we retain the Gaussian dataset’s μ⁡(θ)\mu(\theta) and Σ⁡(θ)\Sigma(\theta), but introduce an equally likely latent scale branch SS:

Pr(S=−1)=Pr(S=+1)=12,X∣θ,S∼𝒩(μ(θ),[1+Sρ(θ)]Σ(θ)).\Pr(S=-1)=\Pr(S=+1)=\tfrac{1}{2},\qquad X\mid\theta,S\sim\mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu(\theta),[1+S\rho(\theta)]\Sigma(\theta)\right). (158)

where ρ⁡(θ)=0.5+0.4​sin⁡[π6​(θ+6)+2.20]\rho(\theta)=0.5+0.4\sin\!\left[\frac{\pi}{6}(\theta+6)+2.20\right]. Because 𝔼⁡[S]=0\mathbb{E}[S]=0, the marginal mean and covariance remain exactly μ⁡(θ)\mu(\theta) and Σ⁡(θ)\Sigma(\theta); ρ⁡(θ)\rho(\theta) therefore changes higher-order structure without changing either of the first two moments, keeping the linear Fisher information the same. The target for the common error panels is the exact mixture full Fisher information,

Ifull(θ)=𝔼X∼pmix(⋅∣θ)[(∂θlogpmix(X∣θ))2].I_{\mathrm{full}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim p^{\mathrm{mix}}(\cdot\mid\theta)}\!\left[\left(\partial_{\theta}\log p^{\mathrm{mix}}(X\mid\theta)\right)^{2}\right]. (159)

We use spacing Δ​θ=0.4\Delta\theta=0.4 and compare Unconstrained Flow, Affine Flow, GKR, and Wishart. The sample-size sweep fixes d=20d=20 and uses N∈{1000,4000,7000,10000,13000}N\in\{1000,4000,7000,10000,13000\}; the dimension sweep fixes N=7000N=7000 and uses d∈{5,20,50,80,110}d\in\{5,20,50,80,110\}.

Gaussian OU dataset: time-local marginals.

xc,r,k=sc​ 0.7​μ​(tk)+LG​(tk)​zc,r,k.x_{c,r,k}=s_{c}\,0.7\mu(t_{k})+L_{\mathrm{G}}(t_{k})z_{c,r,k}. (165)

D.3 Real neural datasets

D.3.1 Mouse V1 static-grating dataset

The mouse V1 static-grating dataset contains six two-photon calcium-imaging sessions (GT1, GT2, GT3, TX38, TX39, and TX40) collected during full-field static-grating presentation [Stringer et al., 2021]. Each trial contributes one population-response vector and one grating orientation, treated modulo π\pi; each session contains about 4000 trials and roughly 20000 simultaneously recorded neurons. Within each session, we form a deterministic, orientation-stratified 64/16/20% training/validation/test split using seed 7. We fit a centered, unwhitened PCA using only the training trials, retain 200 components, and apply the fixed projection to validation and test trials. We chose 200 because it is close to the across-session median of 209 components required to reach a 70% cumulative explained-variance ratio.

We compare five conditional density estimators on the same splits: binning with Ledoit–Wolf covariance (Bin+LW), GKR, the Wishart process, affine flow, and unconstrained flow. Bin+LW uses 16 equal orientation bins of width π/16\pi/16, GKR follows Section D.1.3, and the Wishart process follows Section D.1.4, using the adaptive 16-bin fitting protocol and a full-rank covariance factorization. Both flow models use eight periodic radial-basis features for orientation and a three-hidden-layer MLP of width 256; their fitting follows Section D.1.1.

We evaluate held-out log likelihood on the test split. For Bin+LW, GKR, the Wishart process, and affine flow, we use the fitted mean and covariance to compute Gaussian log likelihood; for unconstrained flow, we use the continuous change-of-variables identity in Eq. (111). This comparison measures conditional density fit rather than direct Fisher-information accuracy.

D.3.2 Allen Brain Observatory two-photon calcium-imaging dataset with drifting gratings

We use two-photon calcium-imaging responses from 11 Allen Brain Observatory visual-cortex recording sessions selected to contain more than 300 recorded neurons [de Vries et al., 2020]. Mice viewed drifting gratings spanning eight motion directions (0∘,45∘,…,315∘0^{\circ},45^{\circ},\ldots,315^{\circ}) and five temporal frequencies (1,2,4,8,1,2,4,8, and 1515 Hz), giving 40 direction–frequency conditions. Each condition has 14–15 repeated trials, corresponding to approximately 560–600 nonblank trials per session. A trial contains 120 frames sampled at 30 Hz and spans four seconds: one second before stimulus onset, two seconds of drifting-grating presentation, and one second after stimulus offset, which also forms the first prestimulus second of the next trial.

For each session, we pool all nonblank observations (conditions ×\times trials ×\times time points) and randomly split into 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% test sets. Trial identity is not used in this split, so frames from the same trial can occur in multiple subsets. We fit a centered, unwhitened PCA to the raw training observations only, retain 95 components, and apply this fixed map to all observations. PCA-95 retains 60.1–89.6% of the training variance across sessions (median 70.2%).

The resulting 95-dimensional observations are conditioned on a categorical index for the 40 direction–frequency combinations and on continuous time. We compare Bin + LW, GKR, the Wishart process, affine flow, and unconstrained flow. Training responses are used for fitting, validation responses for checkpoint or hyperparameter selection, and test responses only for final evaluation.

Supplementary Figure S11 summarizes the responses, held-out likelihood, and time-resolved distance estimates across the 11 two-photon sessions.

D.3.3 Allen Visual Coding Neuropixels dataset

We analyze all 32 recording sessions from the Allen Visual Coding Neuropixels release [Siegle et al., 2021]. These sessions share 40 nonblank drifting-grating conditions formed by eight motion directions and five temporal frequencies. For each session, we retain presentations whose [−1,3)[-1,3)-second analysis window does not overlap an invalid interval. We retain units whose channel lies in VISp, VISl, VISrl, VISam, or VISpm and require presence ratio ≥0.95\geq 0.95, inter-spike-interval violations ≤0.5\leq 0.5, and amplitude cutoff ≤0.1\leq 0.1. The resulting datasets contain 92–373 units and 421–600 presentations per session, with 8–15 presentations per condition.

We count spikes in 40 nonoverlapping 100-ms bins spanning [−1,3)[-1,3) seconds relative to stimulus onset and apply the elementwise square-root transform k↦kk\mapsto\sqrt{k}. Within each session, we fit a centered, unwhitened PCA to all concatenated condition–presentation–time observations before splitting and retain 70 components. These components explain 62.4–95.2% of the variance across sessions (median 72.9%). This is the space we are working on for the rest of analysis. We then randomly divide observation rows into 80% training and 20% test sets; the flow models further divide the outer training rows into 80% training and 20% validation rows.

The models condition on the 40-level direction–frequency index and continuous time. We compare condition-specific Bin + LW, GKR, affine flow, and unconstrained flow. Held-out likelihood is averaged within each condition and then across the 40 conditions, with recording session as the unit of aggregation. For Supplementary Figure S7, we average the 28 unique Jeffreys divergences among the eight directions separately at each temporal frequency within each recording session. Curves and shaded bands show the mean and SEM across the 32 sessions, respectively, with recording session as the aggregation unit. The 4-Hz direction RDMs in Figure 7C are evaluated at the bin centers nearest −0.5-0.5, 1.01.0, and 2.52.5 seconds (realized centers −0.55-0.55, 0.950.95, and 2.452.45 seconds) and averaged across sessions.

D.4 Estimator and dataset for the geometry-template Jeffreys distance

Synthetic dataset.

Let sℓ​(U)s_{\ell}(U) parameterize the boundary of a centered square with side length ℓ\ell, where U∼Unif⁡[0,4]U\sim\operatorname{Unif}[0,4]. For condition cc, we draw

Xc=Rθc​s2​(U)+η,η∼𝒩⁡(0,0.22​I2),(θ1,θ2)=(0,π/4).{X_{c}=R_{\theta_{c}}s_{2}(U)+\eta,\qquad\eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,0.2^{2}I_{2}),\qquad(\theta_{1},\theta_{2})=(0,\pi/4).} (171)

Only XcX_{c} and its condition angle θc\theta_{c} are included in the observed dataset; the perimeter coordinate UU is latent. We generate 200 observations per condition and split each condition into 128 training, 32 validation, and 40 test observations (64/16/20%).

Flow-matching fitting.

Both models start from the same side-length-one square boundary s1​(U)s_{1}(U) convolved with isotropic Gaussian noise of initial scale 0.10.1; thus, the clean source geometry is identical across conditions. We compare two velocity families, each parameterized by a two-hidden-layer MLP of width 64. The similarity-constrained model outputs translation, angular velocity, isotropic scale, and center parameters, so its endpoint map can only translate, rotate, and uniformly rescale the square. The unconstrained model instead maps the response, flow time, and condition directly to a free two-dimensional velocity and may deform the template nonlinearly. We first train each model by Flow Matching along a cosine interpolation path using batch size 256, learning rate 10−310^{-3}, gradient clipping at norm 10, and validation early stopping with patience 1000, while holding the source noise fixed. We then fine-tune by negative log likelihood for 1200 epochs at learning rate 10−410^{-4}, allow a learnable source noise scale σc\sigma_{c}, and retain the checkpoint with the lowest validation NLL.
